slides.title: One craving, sized to four different people
slides.subtitle: Four agents and 34 curated recipes size the same chicken fried rice for each person, with no LLM key needed.
slides.problem: A recipe gives one size for everyone. Daily needs differ, diets rule meals out, and the shopping is left to you.
slides.approach: Four agents turn one craving into one meal: a calorie budget, a safe recipe, a nutrition lookup and a priced shopping list.

findings.headline: Sized to you: 363 to 850 kcal
findings.text: The same chicken fried rice runs from **363 kcal** for an older woman losing weight to **850 kcal** for a large athlete gaining.

findings.headline: On target: 72 of 72 plans
findings.text: Every plan in the project's own **offline benchmark** meets the calorie and macro targets, up from **10**. Median calorie gap **0.4%**.

findings.headline: Fits your limits: 5 of 5
findings.text: Diets, allergies and conditions **rule out recipes or swap ingredients** first. All five guardrail cases behave as designed.

findings.headline: Honest about gaps: 68 of 72
findings.text: **68 of 72** plans include an estimated ingredient, and **11 of 72** are fallback meals. The app labels both.

slides.takeaway: The meal fits the person, and every number says where it came from; the benchmark is the project's own, not a user study.

slides.title: Picking a meal is easy; sizing it to you is not
slides.subtitle: Three questions sit between a craving and a meal you can trust.

items.title: How much?
bullets: Daily budgets in the benchmark run from **1,200 to 4,521 kcal**.
With the app: a budget, then a meal target.

items.title: Is it right for me?
bullets: Asked for pasta, a vegan gets **lentil bolognese** and a coeliac gets **gluten-free pasta**.
With the app: conflicts ruled out or swapped first.

items.title: What do I buy?
bullets: This one pasta means **five ingredients** to find and price.
Today: write a list, guess the cost.
With the app: a list with an estimated total.

slides.takeaway: One request answers all three; the Today lines are this project's framing, not survey results.
slides.question: Why is this worth solving?

notes.purpose: Show the work that sits between a craving and a meal.
script: Most of us know what we feel like eating. The hard part comes after that.
The right amount depends on the person. Diets and conditions change the meal. And even one meal means several ingredients to find and price.
The next section shows how one request answers all three.
Sources: Benchmark budgets: docs/meal_quality/baseline.json; pasta examples: local run, 7 November 2026, no provider keys.

slides.title: The trained model adds only 125 kcal to her day
slides.subtitle: Worked example: an active woman keeping her weight. Her meal target is 28% of the daily budget.
slides.takeaway: The model's R² of 0.996 is for exercise calories, which add 3–10% of the day in these plans.
slides.note: ¹ Exercise inputs use defaults (30 minutes, 100 bpm), and the activity multiplier may already count that exercise.
slides.question: How does it decide how much?

notes.purpose: Follow one person from body to meal target.
script: Body size and activity give about 2,344 kcal a day. The trained model adds 125. Her goal is to maintain, so her budget is 2,469, and one meal gets 28%: 691 kcal.
A weight-loss floor of 1,200 kcal for women and 1,500 for men protects low budgets.
Sources: calorie_expenditure_agent.py; models/calorie_expenditure/metrics.json; local run, 7 November 2026.

slides.title: Hard limits come first, then a relevant recipe
slides.subtitle: A vegan asks for chicken fried rice: the recipes narrow down to one.
slides.takeaway: Safety comes before relevance; across the benchmark, 61 of 72 plans match the craving and 11 fall back with a note.
slides.question: How does it choose the meal?

notes.purpose: Show the funnel from one real request.
script: Of 34 recipes, 13 are safe for a vegan, 5 are relevant to the craving, and one is served.
If nothing is close, you get a standard meal and a note. If nothing is safe, it refuses.
Sources: backend/app/rag/retriever.py; local run, 7 November 2026; docs/meal_quality/baseline.json.

script: Calories had to land within 10% of the target, and each macro inside the adult AMDR range. The same 72 requests run every time.

slides.title: Three fixes took the planner from 10 to 72 of 72
slides.subtitle: Plans meeting both targets on the project's own offline benchmark of 72 requests.
slides.takeaway: The 41 to 47 step moved 11 off-menu requests to fallback meals; a wider check of every recipe by name passes 68 of 68.
slides.note: ¹ Out of 72 benchmark requests. Median calorie gap 0.4%, worst 9.9%; 5 of 5 guardrail cases hold. This shows plans meet targets, not that users prefer them.
slides.question: Did it get better, and why?

script: Resizing each ingredient took it to 41. The relevance gate moved 11 off-menu requests to fallback meals, giving 47. Adding a fat to six recipes and a rounding retry took it to 72.
The fixes were tuned on these 72, so I also asked for every recipe by name: 49 of 68 passed before a further fix, 68 of 68 after.
Sources: docs/7_meal_quality.md §2; docs/meal_quality/baseline.md; DEC-26 to DEC-30.
